section.title: The Appointed Feasts
section.sectionRationale: This chapter gathers Israel's entire liturgical calendar, the weekly Sabbath and the seven annual feasts, into a single sweep, each rehearsing God's past redemption and, as the New Testament will show, anticipating stages of Christ's completed work.
section.thesis: God appoints a calendar of sacred times, weekly Sabbath, Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Weeks, Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and Tabernacles, structuring Israel's whole year around rehearsed remembrance of His redemption and anticipation of its completion.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the weekly Sabbath; Passover and Unleavened Bread; the sheaf of Firstfruits and the counting to the Feast of Weeks; the Feast of Trumpets; the Day of Atonement; and the Feast of Tabernacles, closing the religious year.

units.label: The appointed feasts, and the weekly Sabbath

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and say to them, ‘These are My {{moed|appointed feasts}}, the feasts of the LORD that you are to proclaim as sacred assemblies.
For six days work may be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest, a day of sacred assembly. You must not do any work; wherever you live, it is a Sabbath to the LORD.
These are the LORD’s appointed feasts, the sacred assemblies you are to proclaim at their appointed times.

units.label: Passover and Unleavened Bread
units.note: the year begins with redemption remembered

verses.text: The Passover to the LORD begins at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month.
On the fifteenth day of the same month begins the Feast of Unleavened Bread to the LORD. For seven days you must eat unleavened bread.
On the first day you are to hold a sacred assembly; you are not to do any regular work.
For seven days you are to present an offering made by fire to the LORD. On the seventh day there shall be a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work.’”

units.label: Firstfruits, and the counting to the Feast of Weeks
units.note: the sheaf waved, fifty days counted

verses.text: And the LORD said to Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and say, ‘When you enter the land that I am giving you and you reap its harvest, you are to bring to the priest a sheaf of the {{bikkurim|firstfruits}} of your harvest.
And he shall wave the sheaf before the LORD so that it may be accepted on your behalf; the priest is to wave it on the day after the Sabbath.
On the day you wave the sheaf, you shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering to the LORD,
along with its grain offering of two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, an offering made by fire to the LORD, a pleasing aroma, and its drink offering of a quarter hin of wine.
You must not eat any bread or roasted or new grain until the very day you have brought this offering to your God. This is to be a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live.
From the day after the Sabbath, the day you brought the sheaf of the wave offering, you are to count off seven full weeks.
You shall count off fifty days until the day after the seventh Sabbath, and then present an offering of new grain to the LORD.
Bring two loaves of bread from your dwellings as a wave offering, each made from two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour, baked with leaven, as the firstfruits to the LORD.

Along with the bread you are to present seven unblemished male lambs a year old, one young bull, and two rams. They will be a burnt offering to the LORD, together with their grain offerings and drink offerings, an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
You shall also prepare one male goat as a sin offering and two male lambs a year old as a peace offering.
The priest is to wave the lambs as a wave offering before the LORD, together with the bread of the firstfruits. The bread and the two lambs shall be holy to the LORD for the priest.
On that same day you are to proclaim a sacred assembly, and you must not do any regular work. This is to be a permanent statute wherever you live for the generations to come.

When you reap the harvest of your land, do not reap all the way to the edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest. Leave them for the poor and the foreign resident. I am the LORD your God.’”
The LORD also said to Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and say, ‘On the first day of the seventh month you are to have a day of rest, a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts.
You must not do any regular work, but you are to present an offering made by fire to the LORD.’”
Again the LORD said to Moses,
“The tenth day of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement. You shall hold a sacred assembly and humble yourselves, and present an offering made by fire to the LORD.
On this day you are not to do any work, for it is the Day of Atonement, when atonement is made for you before the LORD your God.
If anyone does not humble himself on this day, he must be cut off from his people.
I will destroy from among his people anyone who does any work on this day.
You are not to do any work at all. This is a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live.
It will be a {{shabbaton|Sabbath of complete rest}} for you, and you shall humble yourselves. From the evening of the ninth day of the month until the following evening you are to keep your Sabbath.”

units.label: The Feast of Tabernacles
units.note: dwelling in booths, rejoicing before the LORD

media.alt: Temporary shelters of branches under an open sky
media.caption: Israel dwells in booths for seven days, remembering the wilderness and rejoicing before the LORD.

verses.text: And the LORD said to Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and say, ‘On the fifteenth day of the seventh month the Feast of {{sukkot|Tabernacles}} to the LORD begins, and it continues for seven days.
On the first day there shall be a sacred assembly. You must not do any regular work.

For seven days you are to present an offering made by fire to the LORD. On the eighth day you are to hold a sacred assembly and present an offering made by fire to the LORD. It is a solemn assembly; you must not do any regular work.

These are the LORD’s appointed feasts, which you are to proclaim as sacred assemblies for presenting offerings by fire to the LORD, burnt offerings and grain offerings, sacrifices and drink offerings, each on its designated day.
These offerings are in addition to the offerings for the LORD’s Sabbaths, and in addition to your gifts, to all your vow offerings, and to all the freewill offerings you give to the LORD.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, after you have gathered the produce of the land, you are to celebrate a feast to the LORD for seven days. There shall be complete rest on the first day and also on the eighth day.

On the first day you are to gather the fruit of majestic trees, the branches of palm trees, and the boughs of leafy trees and of willows of the brook. And you are to rejoice before the LORD your God for seven days.
You are to celebrate this as a feast to the LORD for seven days each year. This is a permanent statute for the generations to come; you are to celebrate it in the seventh month.
You are to dwell in booths for seven days. All the native-born of Israel must dwell in booths,
so that your descendants may know that I made the Israelites dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God.’”
So Moses announced to the Israelites the appointed feasts of the LORD.

moed.gloss: Appointed time or appointed feast, from a root meaning to fix or designate. These are not spontaneous holidays but fixed dates God Himself sets on Israel's calendar, structuring their whole year around remembering His redemption.

bikkurim.gloss: Firstfruits, the earliest and best portion of the harvest, offered before the rest could be used, acknowledging that the whole harvest, and the land itself, belongs to God. Paul later applies this exact term to Christ's resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:20.

shabbaton.gloss: A Sabbath of complete rest, an intensified form of the ordinary word for Sabbath. Applied here to the Day of Atonement, it marks that day as carrying the same total cessation of work as the weekly Sabbath itself.

sukkot.gloss: Booths or temporary shelters, giving the Feast of Tabernacles its name. Dwelling in these fragile structures for seven days rehearsed Israel's wilderness dependence on God and anticipated, in John's Gospel, the Word becoming flesh and tabernacling among us.

basic.context: This chapter lists Israel's entire yearly calendar of sacred times: the weekly Sabbath, Passover, Unleavened Bread, the Firstfruits sheaf, the Feast of Weeks fifty days later, the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Tabernacles.
basic.hermeneutics: This is Israel's specific old covenant festival calendar. Colossians 2:16-17 explicitly calls these feasts a shadow of what was to come, whose substance belongs to Christ; Christians are not obligated to observe them, though the pattern of structured, communal worship remembering God's redemption continues and finds its center in Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: Each mo'ed, appointed time, is fixed by God, not chosen by Israel. The bikkurim, firstfruits, wave offering anticipates the full harvest to come, and Paul uses this exact term of Christ's resurrection. The sukkot, booths, of the final feast recall the wilderness and anticipate God's dwelling with His people.
basic.typology: Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, and Weeks are explicitly interpreted by the New Testament as fulfilled in Christ's death, sinless purity, resurrection, and the Spirit's outpouring; Tabernacles anticipates both the incarnation and the final ingathering when God's dwelling will be with man forever.
basic.christ: Paul writes plainly, Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed, 1 Corinthians 5:7, and calls Him the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20. Acts 2 records the Spirit poured out at the very feast of Weeks, fifty days after the resurrection, gathering the first great harvest of souls into the church.
basic.god: God is a God of appointed times, not disorder; He structures His people's whole year around remembering His redemption from Egypt and anticipating its final completion, showing that worship is meant to shape all of time, not merely isolated moments.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 5:7-8 calls Christ our Passover. 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 names Him the firstfruits of the resurrection. Acts 2:1-41 records Pentecost's fulfillment. John 7:37-39 shows Jesus offering living water at the Feast of Tabernacles. Revelation 21:3 promises God's dwelling will finally be with man.
basic.oneStory: Israel's whole year was structured to rehearse God's redemption and lean forward to its completion. Every feast finds its true content in Christ: our Passover, our unleavened purity, our firstfruits from the dead, our Pentecost outpouring, and the coming day when God's dwelling with His people, pictured in booths, becomes permanent and complete.

context.literary:
Chapters 21 and 22 dealt with holy persons and holy things; chapter 23 turns to holy time. The chapter is built from five divine speeches, each introduced by 'the LORD said to Moses,' verses 1, 9, 23, 26 and 33. The first covers the Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread; the second the firstfruits sheaf and Weeks; the third Trumpets; the fourth the Day of Atonement; the fifth Tabernacles.

The chapter has two headings. Verse 2 announces 'These are My appointed feasts,' and after the Sabbath is described, verse 4 begins again: 'These are the LORD's appointed feasts.' The Sabbath stands apart as the weekly rhythm underneath the annual ones. A matching summary in verses 37 and 38 closes the list, and then verses 39 to 43 return to Tabernacles to add the palm branches, the rejoicing and the booths, as though the chapter could not end without that festival's joy.

The number seven runs through the calendar. The seventh day is the Sabbath. Unleavened Bread lasts seven days. Weeks comes after seven full weeks. The seventh month holds three feasts: Trumpets on the first day, Atonement on the tenth, Tabernacles from the fifteenth for seven days. The whole year is shaped by the pattern of the creation week, Genesis 2:2-3.

The year also divides into two halves. The spring feasts of the first month gather around Passover and the grain harvest. The autumn feasts of the seventh month gather around atonement and the fruit harvest. Between them, verse 22 repeats the gleaning law of Leviticus 19:9, so that at the height of harvest joy Israel remembers the poor and the foreigner.

The repeated phrases shape how the feasts are kept: 'sacred assembly,' 'you must not do any regular work,' 'an offering made by fire,' and 'a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live.' The last phrase, in verses 14, 21 and 31, reaches beyond the tabernacle to every Israelite home.
context.historical:
Israel's calendar was lunar, and the feasts were tied to the agricultural year of the land. The first month, called Abib in Exodus 23:15 and later Nisan, Esther 3:7, fell in spring. The sheaf of firstfruits came from the first grain to ripen, and Ruth's story shows how the barley harvest came first and the wheat harvest after, Ruth 1:22 and 2:23. The Feast of Weeks is tied in Exodus 34:22 to 'the firstfruits of the wheat harvest.' Tabernacles came 'after you have gathered the produce of the land,' verse 39, the grape and olive harvest of autumn, which is why it was also called the Feast of Ingathering, Exodus 23:16.

Three of these feasts, Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Tabernacles, were pilgrim feasts, when 'all your men are to appear before the LORD your God in the place He will choose,' Deuteronomy 16:16. Leviticus 23 presupposes the sanctuary but also speaks of what is kept 'wherever you live.'

Several commands look ahead to life in Canaan. The sheaf is brought 'when you enter the land,' verse 10, and no new grain may be eaten until it is offered, verse 14. Joshua 5:10-12 records the first Passover in the land: the day after it, Israel ate 'unleavened bread and roasted grain from the produce of the land,' and the manna stopped.

Israel's history records long neglect and occasional recovery of the feasts. Hezekiah and Josiah held great Passovers, 2 Chronicles 30:1 and 2 Kings 23:22. Solomon dedicated the temple 'at the feast in the seventh month,' 1 Kings 8:2. After the exile the returned community rediscovered the booths, and Nehemiah 8:17 says that 'from the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this.' By the first century the Day of Atonement could simply be called 'the Fast,' Acts 27:9, and Jerusalem filled at Pentecost with 'God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven,' Acts 2:5.
context.canonical:
The calendar of Leviticus 23 is restated and filled out elsewhere in the Law: Exodus 23:14-17 and 34:22-23 give the three pilgrim feasts, Numbers 28 and 29 list the offerings for each day, and Deuteronomy 16 stresses rejoicing and the inclusion of 'the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widows,' Deuteronomy 16:14. The prophets then use the feasts to speak of the future. Hosea warns, 'I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast,' Hosea 12:9. Zechariah sees the nations going up 'year after year to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts, and to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles,' Zechariah 14:16. Isaiah foresees a great ram's horn gathering the exiles to worship on the holy mountain, Isaiah 27:13.

The Gospels are structured around these feasts. John's Gospel marks Jesus' ministry by them: Passovers in John 2:13, 6:4 and 11:55, and Tabernacles in John 7:2, where 'on the last and greatest day of the feast' Jesus cries out, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37. The crucifixion takes place at Passover, and John notes that none of Jesus' bones were broken, John 19:36, recalling the Passover lamb of Exodus 12:46. Jesus rose 'on the first day of the week,' John 20:1, the day after the Sabbath, when the firstfruits sheaf was waved.

Paul reads the spring feasts christologically: 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us keep the feast,' 1 Corinthians 5:7-8, and 'Christ the firstfruits,' 1 Corinthians 15:23. Acts 2 sets the coming of the Spirit on 'the day of Pentecost.' Hebrews interprets the Day of Atonement at length, Hebrews 9:7-12. Colossians 2:16-17 calls festivals 'a shadow of the things to come,' while Revelation's great multitude holding palm branches, Revelation 7:9, and its announcement that 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3, echo the imagery of Tabernacles.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel's time to belong to God. By fixing these feasts as 'My appointed feasts,' verse 2, God claimed the calendar. Israel was not to live by the rhythms of the nations' festivals, many of them tied to fertility gods, but by a year that retold the LORD's acts and acknowledged Him as Giver of the harvest.

He meant each feast to join memory and gratitude. Passover and Unleavened Bread recalled the night of the exodus. Tabernacles recalled the wilderness, 'so that your descendants may know that I made the Israelites dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt,' verse 43. The harvest feasts gave thanks for the land. Faith was to be formed not only by hearing but by eating unleavened bread, waving sheaves, and sleeping under branches.

The feasts also taught the order of the spiritual life. No new grain was eaten until the first was given, verse 14. The year's climax was not a festival of plenty alone but the Day of Atonement followed by the joy of Tabernacles. Cleansing comes before rejoicing, and humbling before celebration.

Finally, Moses meant the feasts to bind the community together. They were 'sacred assemblies,' public gatherings. The gleaning law of verse 22, set in the middle of the harvest feasts, made sure the poor and the foreigner shared in the harvest. Worship and justice were bound together.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter prescribes Israel's festival calendar, with its dates, offerings and rest days, as a covenant obligation. Christians are not bound to keep it. Paul says no one should judge believers 'with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath,' because 'these are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ,' Colossians 2:16-17. He warns the Galatians against treating the observance of 'special days and months and seasons and years' as necessary, Galatians 4:10-11, while in Romans 14:5-6 he allows believers to differ over days so long as each acts 'to the Lord.'

What carries forward is instructive. God's people still need regular rhythms of rest and gathered worship, Hebrews 10:25. They still remember a redemption, now centred on the cross and resurrection, in the Lord's Supper and on the Lord's Day. They still give the first and best to God, and they still include the poor in their joy. The feasts teach Christians how to read the gospel: as a Passover, a firstfruits, a harvest of the Spirit, an atonement, and a coming dwelling with God.

debates.question: How exact and detailed should Christians be in mapping each feast to a New Testament fulfilment?

views.label: Confident, textually anchored typology for feasts the New Testament explicitly interprets
views.case: Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits and Weeks are directly connected to Christ's death, the call to holiness, His resurrection and the Spirit's outpouring by the New Testament writers themselves, 1 Corinthians 5:7-8, 15:20-23 and Acts 2:1. These connections rest on apostolic authority, not speculation. Hebrews 9 does the same for the Day of Atonement.

views.label: A prophetic timetable in the autumn feasts
views.case: Some interpreters, especially in dispensational traditions, argue that since the spring feasts were fulfilled at Christ's first coming in order, the autumn feasts must be fulfilled at His second: Trumpets in the trumpet call of His return, 1 Thessalonians 4:16, Atonement in Israel's national repentance, Zechariah 12:10, and Tabernacles in the kingdom, Zechariah 14:16.

views.label: More caution for feasts without explicit New Testament interpretation
views.case: Others note that Trumpets and Tabernacles are not assigned a specific fulfilment event by the New Testament. The broad themes, the trumpet at Christ's return, God dwelling with man, fit naturally, but detailed timelines built on the autumn feasts go beyond what Scripture says.

debates.bearing: Confidence should track the New Testament's own explicit statements. Where Scripture identifies a fulfilment, that reading carries real authority. Where it does not, believers can hold suggested connections as reasonable themes rather than a fixed calendar of future events.

debates.question: Which 'Sabbath' is meant in 'the day after the Sabbath,' verses 11 and 15?

views.label: The weekly Sabbath
views.case: The word Sabbath in verse 3 means the seventh day, and verse 15 counts 'seven full weeks' to 'the day after the seventh Sabbath,' verse 16, which reads most naturally as a count of weekly Sabbaths. On this view the sheaf was always waved on the first day of the week, and Weeks always fell on that day as well. In the late Second Temple period this was the position of Sadducean circles.

views.label: The first day of Unleavened Bread as a rest day
views.case: Others take 'Sabbath' to mean the festival rest day of verse 7, the fifteenth of the month, so that the sheaf was waved on the sixteenth whatever the day of the week. This was the Pharisaic view and became standard in later Jewish practice. It fixes the sheaf to the Passover date rather than to the week.

debates.bearing: The question cannot be settled with certainty from the text alone, though the counting language of verses 15 and 16 leans toward the weekly Sabbath. In the year of the crucifixion the Gospels place the resurrection on 'the first day of the week,' John 20:1, and Paul calls Christ 'the firstfruits,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. However the ancient calendar was reckoned, the New Testament sees the risen Christ as the sheaf that guarantees the harvest.

debates.question: Should Christians observe the feasts of Leviticus 23 today?

views.label: Not as an obligation, since the shadow has given way to the substance
views.case: Colossians 2:16-17 and Galatians 4:10-11 treat the festival calendar as fulfilled in Christ. The church from its earliest days gathered on 'the first day of the week,' Acts 20:7, and kept the Lord's Supper rather than the Passover meal. Requiring the feasts would imply that Christ's work is incomplete.

views.label: As a permitted and instructive practice
views.case: Others note that Paul himself hurried to reach Jerusalem 'by the day of Pentecost,' Acts 20:16, and that Romans 14:5-6 permits observing days to the Lord. Some Christians, especially Jewish believers, keep the feasts as a way of remembering God's faithfulness and seeing Christ in the calendar, without treating them as necessary for salvation.

debates.bearing: The New Testament forbids imposing the feasts as a requirement and permits freedom in keeping them to the Lord. What matters is that no observance is made a condition of standing before God, and that believers recognise the substance of every feast in Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's key word, mo'ed, 'appointed feast,' comes from a root meaning to fix or appoint. It is the same word used in Genesis 1:14, where the lights in the sky are given 'to mark the seasons,' mo'adim. It is also the word in the name 'Tent of Meeting,' 'ohel mo'ed, the tent where God met His people at the time and place He appointed. An appointed feast is a meeting in time as the tent was a meeting in space.

Each feast is a miqra qodesh, 'sacred assembly,' from qara, to call or proclaim. Verse 2 plays on it: the feasts 'that you are to proclaim,' tiqre'u, 'as sacred assemblies,' miqra'e qodesh. These are called gatherings, summoned by proclamation. The New Testament word for the church, ekklesia, is likewise built on a verb of calling.

The chapter distinguishes two levels of rest. On the weekly Sabbath and the Day of Atonement no work at all is allowed, kol mela'khah, 'any work,' verses 3, 28 and 31. On the other feast days what is forbidden is mele'khet avodah, 'regular work,' verses 7, 8, 21, 25, 35 and 36, the ordinary labour of one's trade. Within this chapter only the Sabbath and the Day of Atonement are called shabbat shabbaton, 'a Sabbath of complete rest,' verses 3 and 32. The Day of Atonement is treated with the full weight of the Sabbath.

The sheaf of verse 10 is an omer, and it comes from reshit qetsirkhem, 'the first of your harvest.' The word reshit, beginning or first part, is the word of Genesis 1:1, 'In the beginning.' The noun bikkurim, 'firstfruits,' is used for the leavened loaves of Weeks in verses 17 and 20. Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 15:20, aparche, is the word the Septuagint commonly uses for the first portion given to God. The first sheaf sanctified the whole harvest; the risen Christ is the first of a resurrection harvest.

The Feast of Weeks is reached by counting 'fifty days,' verse 16. From the Greek word for fiftieth comes its New Testament name, Pentecost, Acts 2:1.

The Feast of Trumpets in verse 24 is literally a zikhron teru'ah, 'a memorial of blasting' or, as the BSB footnote has it, 'a memorial of shouting.' Teru'ah is the word for a loud blast or shout, used of battle cries and festive shouting. Numbers 10:10 likewise speaks of trumpets blown over the sacrifices 'to serve as a reminder,' the same idea of memorial before God.

On the Day of Atonement Israel was to 'humble yourselves,' verses 27, 29 and 32, literally 'afflict your souls,' as the BSB footnote notes. The same idiom describes fasting in Psalm 35:13, 'I humbled myself with fasting,' and in Isaiah 58:3 and 58:5. The day's name, yom hakkippurim, uses a plural, 'the day of atonements,' gathering up the many acts of cleansing described in Leviticus 16.

Finally, the booths of verse 42 are sukkot, temporary shelters of branches, the word that gave the town Succoth its name, Genesis 33:17. The Septuagint calls the festival the feast of skenai, tents, and John uses the related verb when he writes that the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, literally pitched His tent. In John 7:2 the festival is called by a Greek compound meaning tent pitching.

typology.type: Passover, the fourteenth day of the first month, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: The Passover lamb was killed at twilight, and its blood marked the houses that would be spared. Paul writes, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. John places the crucifixion at the Passover and notes that Jesus' legs were not broken, 'so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: Not one of His bones will be broken,' John 19:36, recalling Exodus 12:46. Jesus Himself reinterpreted the Passover meal at the Last Supper, saying He would not eat it again 'until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God,' Luke 22:16. The type falls short in that the first Passover delivered from Egypt; Christ's delivers from sin and death.

typology.type: The Feast of Unleavened Bread, seven days without leaven, verses 6-8
typology.fulfillment: Israel removed all leaven from its houses and ate 'the bread of affliction,' Deuteronomy 16:3, remembering the haste of the exodus. Paul turns the feast into a picture of the Christian life: 'Get rid of the old leaven, that you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. The order matters. The lamb is killed first, then the leaven is removed. Holiness is the response to redemption, not its cause. The escalation is that the seven days become the whole of life, lived 'with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth,' 1 Corinthians 5:8.

typology.type: The sheaf of firstfruits, waved the day after the Sabbath, verses 10-14
typology.fulfillment: The first sheaf of the harvest was waved before the LORD, and no one could eat the new grain until it had been offered. It was a pledge that the rest of the harvest would follow. Jesus rose 'early on the first day of the week,' John 20:1, and Paul writes, 'Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, then 'Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him,' 15:23. The escalation is enormous: a sheaf of barley becomes the risen body of the Son, the guarantee of the resurrection of all His people.

typology.type: The Feast of Weeks, fifty days later, with new grain and leavened loaves, verses 15-21
typology.fulfillment: Fifty days after the sheaf, Israel offered two leavened loaves as firstfruits of the wheat harvest. At that very feast, 'when the day of Pentecost came,' the Spirit was poured out on the disciples, Acts 2:1-4, and 'about three thousand were added to the believers that day,' Acts 2:41, a first harvest of the church. The leavened loaves, unlike the unleavened bread of Passover, may fittingly picture a people not yet perfect but accepted. Paul calls the Spirit 'the firstfruits,' Romans 8:23, and James calls believers 'a kind of firstfruits of His creation,' James 1:18.

typology.type: The Day of Atonement, the tenth day of the seventh month, verses 26-32
typology.fulfillment: Once a year the high priest entered the Most Holy Place with blood, and the people humbled themselves while atonement was made. Hebrews says that only the high priest entered, 'once a year, and never without blood,' Hebrews 9:7, and that Christ 'entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption,' Hebrews 9:12. The type falls short in its repetition: 'those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins,' Hebrews 10:3. Christ's single offering ends the need for another Day of Atonement, and His people rest in it.

typology.type: The Feast of Tabernacles, dwelling in temporary shelters, verses 33-43
typology.fulfillment: For seven days Israel lived in booths, remembering that God had sheltered them in the wilderness, and rejoiced at the ingathering. John writes that 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, using a verb that means to pitch a tent. At Tabernacles Jesus offered living water to the thirsty, John 7:37-39. Revelation shows a multitude from every nation 'holding palm branches,' Revelation 7:9, and announces, 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3. The booths were temporary; the final dwelling is forever, and the harvest gathered is the nations.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by its order. The year begins with a lamb, moves to a sheaf raised the day after the Sabbath, then to a harvest fifty days later. The New Testament walks through the same sequence with astonishing precision. Jesus dies at Passover, John 19:14; rises on the first day of the week, John 20:1; and fifty days later, 'when the day of Pentecost came,' the Spirit is poured out, Acts 2:1. Paul names the correspondences himself: 'Christ, our Passover lamb,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and 'Christ the firstfruits,' 1 Corinthians 15:23.

It leads to Christ by the Day of Atonement. The holiest day of Israel's year required humbling and complete rest while the high priest made atonement. Hebrews says Christ 'appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself,' Hebrews 9:26. The day that had to be repeated annually is replaced by one day that never needs repeating. And the command to do no work on that day, verses 28 to 31, becomes a picture of grace: atonement is received, not achieved.

It leads to Christ by Tabernacles. The booths recalled the wilderness, where God dwelt among His people in a tent. John opens his Gospel by saying the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, the eternal Son pitching His tent in human flesh. On the last and greatest day of that very feast Jesus stood and cried, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37, and soon after said, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12. Later Jewish practice at the feast, recorded in the Mishnah, included water pouring and great lamps in the temple courts, which makes those words especially pointed, though John does not describe the ceremonies himself.

It leads to Christ by the Sabbath at the head of the list. Every feast is set on the foundation of rest. Jesus said, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28, and called Himself 'Lord even of the Sabbath,' Mark 2:28. Hebrews 4:9-10 says 'a Sabbath rest' remains for God's people, entered by faith.

The autumn feasts of Trumpets and Tabernacles are not given a single fulfilment event in the New Testament, and humility is fitting there. Yet the trumpet sounds again at Christ's return, 1 Thessalonians 4:16, and the dwelling of God with humanity is the last word of the Bible's story, Revelation 21:3. The shadow, Colossians 2:17 says, is cast by His body.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is that He is Lord of time. He made the lights 'to mark the seasons,' Genesis 1:14, and here He fixes the seasons of worship. Time is not a neutral container that human beings fill as they like; it is God's gift, and He claims its rhythm. 'These are My appointed feasts,' verse 2. The God who rested on the seventh day, Genesis 2:2-3, invites His people into that rest every week.

He is the God who acts in history and wants it remembered. The feasts are tied to real events: the night of the exodus, the years of wandering, the harvests of a land He gave. Faith in Israel was historical, not mythic. The nations' festivals often celebrated the cycles of nature and the gods behind them; Israel's feasts celebrated the LORD who had acted at particular times for a particular people.

He is the Giver of the harvest. The firstfruits sheaf and the loaves of Weeks acknowledge that the land and its yield belong to Him. The command not to eat new grain until the first was offered, verse 14, teaches that God is honoured first, not last.

He is the God who makes atonement. The chapter's most solemn day is not about what Israel does for God but about what is done for Israel before Him: 'atonement is made for you before the LORD your God,' verse 28. His holiness demands cleansing; His mercy provides it.

He is a God of joy. The chapter ends not at the Day of Atonement but five days later with a command: 'you are to rejoice before the LORD your God for seven days,' verse 40. Atonement leads to celebration. Deuteronomy adds that the whole community, including 'the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widows,' is to share it, Deuteronomy 16:14, and the gleaning law of verse 22 already makes room for them in the harvest. God's joy is generous and wide.

He holds together remembrance and hope. Every feast looks back to what God has done and forward to a greater fulfilment. The God who kept His appointments in the exodus will keep them again, and He did, at a Passover in Jerusalem and a Pentecost fifty days later.

For worship, this chapter calls believers to give their time to God, to remember His acts, to rest in the atonement He provided, and to rejoice together before Him with open hands toward the poor.

crossReferences.note: The lights in the sky are made 'to mark the seasons and days and years.' The word for seasons is mo'adim, the same word as the 'appointed feasts' of Leviticus 23:2. From creation God built the calendar that Israel's worship would fill.

The original institution of Unleavened Bread commands the removal of leaven for seven days and a sacred assembly on the first and seventh days. Leviticus 23:6-8 restates it in the context of the whole year, tying the feast to the night Israel left Egypt.

Israel's first Passover in Canaan is followed by eating 'unleavened bread and roasted grain from the produce of the land,' and the manna ceases. The provision of Leviticus 23:10-14 for entering the land comes true, and God's people move from wilderness bread to the harvest He promised.

The returned exiles find the command to dwell in booths and keep Tabernacles with great rejoicing, 'from the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day' unmatched. The law of Leviticus 23:40-43 is recovered after long neglect as the word is read.

The prophet sees survivors from the nations going up year after year 'to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts, and to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles.' Israel's harvest feast becomes a picture of the nations gathered to God, carrying Leviticus 23:34-43 into the prophetic hope.

On 'the last and greatest day' of Tabernacles Jesus invites the thirsty to come to Him and drink, speaking of the Spirit. He presents Himself as the fulfilment of the feast that recalled God's provision in the wilderness, Leviticus 23:43, including water from the rock.

John says Jesus' bones were not broken 'so that the Scripture would be fulfilled,' recalling the Passover lamb of Exodus 12:46. The crucifixion at the Passover season of Leviticus 23:5 is presented as the true Passover sacrifice.

Paul calls Christ 'our Passover lamb' and tells the church to 'keep the feast' with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. He moves from Passover to Unleavened Bread just as Leviticus 23:5-6 does, and applies the removal of leaven to the church's holiness.

Christ is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' and 'then at His coming, those who belong to Him.' The sheaf of Leviticus 23:10-11, offered before the harvest could be eaten, becomes Paul's image for the risen Christ as the pledge of the resurrection.

'When the day of Pentecost came,' the Spirit was poured out, and about three thousand were added that day. The Feast of Weeks, the harvest offering of Leviticus 23:15-21, becomes the day of the first great harvest of the church.

Only the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, once a year and never without blood, but Christ entered once for all by His own blood, securing eternal redemption. The Day of Atonement of Leviticus 23:26-32 is fulfilled in a single, final offering.

No one should judge believers regarding a feast, a New Moon or a Sabbath, because 'these are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ.' Paul names the whole calendar of Leviticus 23 as a shadow and Christ as its substance.

A loud voice declares, 'the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.' The Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel lived in booths remembering God's wilderness presence, Leviticus 23:42-43, reaches its end in God's permanent dwelling with His people.

study.oneStory:
Time itself is part of creation. On the fourth day God set lights in the sky 'to mark the seasons,' Genesis 1:14, and on the seventh He rested and blessed the day, Genesis 2:3. The calendar was meant to be a rhythm of work, rest and communion with God. After the fall, time became the measure of toil and death, and the nations filled their calendars with festivals to gods of fertility and harvest.

Leviticus 23 gives God's people a redeemed calendar. It begins with the Sabbath, recalling creation's rest. It moves through Passover, recalling the night of redemption from Egypt, and through harvests that confess the land as God's gift. Its climax is the Day of Atonement, when a sinful people is cleansed, followed by the joy of Tabernacles, when Israel remembers that God sheltered them in the wilderness. The whole year rehearses the story from creation through redemption to the joy of God's presence.

Israel neglected the calendar for long stretches, and even when it kept the feasts the sacrifices had to be repeated. The Day of Atonement came back every year as 'an annual reminder of sins,' Hebrews 10:3. The feasts pointed forward to something they could not themselves accomplish.

In Christ the calendar is fulfilled. He is the Passover lamb, the firstfruits raised the day after the Sabbath, the giver of the Spirit at Pentecost, the High Priest who made atonement once for all, and the Word who pitched His tent among us. The church lives in the time between the firstfruits and the full harvest, gathering on the first day of the week and waiting for the final trumpet, 1 Corinthians 15:52.

The story ends in a feast. The multitude from every nation stands before the throne with palm branches, Revelation 7:9, as Israel once waved branches at Tabernacles. God's dwelling is with humanity, Revelation 21:3, and the booths of branches give way to a city that will never be taken down. The final harvest is gathered, the Sabbath rest that remains for God's people is entered, Hebrews 4:9, and the joy that Leviticus 23:40 commanded for seven days becomes everlasting.

quiz.q: How many days did the weekly cycle include before the Sabbath of complete rest, according to verse 3?

options.text: Six days of work, followed by a seventh day Sabbath of complete rest.
options.note: Verse 3 states this pattern explicitly.

options.text: Ten days of work, followed by one day of rest.
options.note: The text specifies a six day and seventh day pattern, not a ten day cycle.

options.text: No regular weekly pattern is described.
options.note: Verse 3 explicitly describes the six and seven day pattern.

options.text: Three days of work, followed by four days of rest.
options.note: Verse 3 specifies six days of work and one day of rest.

quiz.q: When was the sheaf of firstfruits waved before the LORD, according to verse 11?

options.text: On the day after the Sabbath, during the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
options.note: Verse 11 specifies this timing directly.

options.text: Exactly fifty days after Passover.
options.note: Fifty days describes the timing of the Feast of Weeks, not the firstfruits sheaf, which came earlier.

options.text: At the very end of the agricultural year.
options.note: The firstfruits offering came near the start of harvest, not its end.

options.text: No specific timing is given.
options.note: Verse 11 gives a specific timing for this offering.

quiz.q: How many days after the firstfruits sheaf was the Feast of Weeks to be celebrated?

options.text: Fifty days.
options.note: Verse 16 specifies counting fifty days until this feast.

options.text: Seven days.
options.note: Seven days describes the length of Unleavened Bread and Tabernacles, not the interval to the Feast of Weeks.

options.text: One hundred days.
options.note: Verse 16 specifies fifty days, not one hundred.

options.text: No interval is specified.
options.note: Verses 15-16 specify this fifty day count explicitly.

quiz.q: What were the Israelites commanded to do for seven days during the Feast of Tabernacles?

options.text: Dwell in booths and rejoice before the LORD, remembering their time in the wilderness.
options.note: Verses 40-43 specify this practice and its stated purpose.

options.text: Fast completely for the entire seven days.
options.note: Fasting or humbling is specifically associated with the Day of Atonement, not Tabernacles, which involves rejoicing.

options.text: Remain silent and avoid all public gathering.
options.note: The text specifically calls for sacred assemblies and rejoicing, not silence or isolation.

options.text: No specific practice is commanded for this feast.
options.note: Verses 40-43 give specific and detailed instructions.

quiz.q: How does 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 connect Christ to the Feast of Firstfruits?

options.text: It calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, guaranteeing the resurrection of all who belong to Him.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 makes this connection directly.

options.text: It denies any connection between Christ and the Old Testament feasts.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 draws this connection explicitly rather than denying it.

options.text: It applies the firstfruits language only to Old Testament harvests, never to Christ.
options.note: Paul explicitly applies this very term to Christ's own resurrection.

options.text: There is no New Testament reference to firstfruits at all.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 15:20 uses this exact term of Christ.

questions: God structured Israel's entire year around remembering His redemption. What regular rhythms, daily, weekly, yearly, shape your own remembrance of what God has done for you in Christ?

Passover looked back to a specific historical rescue; the church now looks back to a specific historical resurrection. How present and vivid is Easter, not just as a date but as a lived reality, in your ordinary week to week faith?

The Feast of Weeks required Israel to wait, count, and anticipate before the harvest offering came. Where in your life is God asking you to wait faithfully for something you cannot yet see or receive?

Tabernacles called Israel to dwell in fragile, temporary shelters, remembering their dependence on God in the wilderness. What comforts or securities in your life would be hardest to live without for even a week?

The whole festal calendar leans forward to a future, final ingathering when God's dwelling will be permanently with His people. How does that future hope shape the way you face the hardships of today?

translationNotes.note: The day after the Sabbath became a point of significant later debate among Jewish interpreters, some understanding it as the day after the weekly Sabbath during Unleavened Bread week, others as the day after the first day of the feast itself, which affected the calculated date of the Feast of Weeks.

Announced by trumpet blasts translates a phrase, zikron teruah, that can also be rendered a memorial of trumpet blasts or a shout, giving this feast its traditional name, though the text does not explain what the trumpets specifically commemorated.

The fruit of majestic trees and branches gathered on the first day of Tabernacles later developed, in Jewish tradition, into the specific set of four species carried in procession, though the text itself leaves the exact identification of some plants open.
